newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian parliament lays claim to Ukrainian port.
newsitem.headline: Russian parliament lays claim to Ukrainian port.

text.p: The upper house of Russia's parliament on Thursday publicly laid claim to Ukraine's Black Sea naval port of Sevastopol, saying it was part of Russia and Kiev had no legal right to govern it.

The Federation Council, in a move likely to cause a storm of protest in Kiev and further poison mistrustful relations between the two governments, endorsed the demand that Ukraine surrender the city by a majority of 110 to 14.
There was no immediate reaction in Kiev to the territorial claim, which is not binding on President Boris Yeltsin or the Russian government.
But it comes at a sensitive moment, with talks between Moscow and Kiev on Sevastopol and the disputed Black Sea Fleet deadlocked and with NATO expansion plans causing further tensions.

Senior Ukrainian officials have openly warned Moscow in the past month that Kiev may raise any Russian territorial claims at the United Nations and have pointedly begun saying they cannot rule out a possible application for NATO membership in future.
Thursday's buildup in pressure from Moscow was likely to increase pro-Western and anti-Russian trends in Kiev.

"Unilateral actions by the Ukrainian side aimed at tearing away from Russia a part of its territory (Sevastopol) are not only illegal under international law, but also directly damage Russia's security," the Federation Council resolution said.

Ukraine's actions "are preventing the establishment of good neighbourly and profitable relations between two fraternal peoples and are lowering the authority of both countries in the international arena", it said.
The Council also set up a special commission to prepare a draft law on the status of Sevastopol, a historic Russian naval base founded in the 1780s when Moscow conquered Crimea.
The Kremlin ruled Ukraine for more than three centuries, but it recognised Ukrainian independence and territorial integrity at the time of the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991.
However Crimea, transferred to Ukraine from Russia in 1954, is mostly populated by ethnic Russians who have little loyalty to Kiev and look to Moscow for protection.
The last round of talks on the disputed Black Sea Fleet collapsed in acrimony on November 6, when a Russian delegation left Kiev without attending a final dinner.
The two governments have been discussing a lease agreement under which Russia would keep the biggest share of the fleet and continue to use Sevastopol as a base.
But talks have foundered over Russian demands that the Ukrainian navy should base itself elsewhere, a demand which Kiev has rejected.
Both documents approved by the Federation Council were proposed by Moscow's powerful mayor Yuri Luzhkov, a Yeltsin ally who is widely touted as a possible successor to the president.
Luzhkov argued that the 1954 Kremlin decision to transfer the Crimean peninsula from Russia to Ukraine did not include Sevastopol which had a special status at the time.

Yeltsin has promised to visit Kiev to sign a friendship treaty with President Leonid Kuchma, but has postponed his trip six times. He has recently insisted that the Ukrainian and Russian prime ministers first sign an agreement on the Black Sea Fleet before he will sign the treaty.
In a Russian television interview last Saturday Kuchma suggested going ahead with the treaty and settling the Fleet issue later, but a Kremlin spokesman rejected this option.
The Federation Council vote followed a similar resolution several weeks ago on Sevastopol by the lower house, the State Duma, which infuriated Ukraine's parliament and government.
Ukraine protested officially to Moscow, where the foreign ministry denied that Russia had any territorial claims on its neighbour.
